Foo Camp · October 2026

A thinking harness

Adam Davidson · slides and talk text

Read the full session transcript → (No names or identifying information, per Foo’s Chatham House rule.)

01

Quick intro. Five minutes, then we talk — and maybe build one on paper.

02

I’ve worked in very different editorial cultures. They all do the same basic job: take a vague idea, a provocation, a news event — something that isn’t a story yet — and turn it into something worth telling. Daily NPR pushed hard toward execution: get it out today. Other places gave ideas more room to linger before we committed. The point isn’t which is better. It’s that the conditions shape the thoughts that come out.

03

Your editor — the person you just call “your editor” — is your thought partner and daily check-in: what stories to do, how, when, and then getting them across the finish line. They work for the top editor, whose job is the big picture: are there fundamental questions you’ve missed? Have the two of you come to believe a story that might not be as true as you think? How does it fit the flow of the magazine or the show? Then line editors and copy editors, going comma by comma. Fact-checkers, making sure it’s true. And colleagues, who serve different functions: the wild, creative one you go to for a big new idea; the rigorous, meticulous one who challenges you; and the one who doesn’t know the topic, who shows you where you’ve overcomplicated things or lost the average person.

04

I use AI as a thought partner all the time, and I keep hitting a mismatch between the kind of help I need and the kind I get.

05

Even making this five-minute talk: some conversations with LLMs were wonderful. Others kept trying to force me to execute, kept raising objections that didn’t matter, and one seemed weirdly committed to never saying anything negative about NPR. Every one of those moments, I was managing the collaborator instead of thinking about the idea.

06

Here’s what actually happens. I start out excited, in flow, ideas coming fast. Then the model does the wrong kind of help a few times in a row, and I go from flow to frustrated to genuinely angry — arguing with a tool instead of thinking about the idea. Newsrooms can do this to you too; bad editors are real. That is not the part of the newsroom I want to copy.

07

So here’s the idea. You choose how you want to think with the AI right now. The harness holds that choice — it doesn’t drift back to finishing the assignment. And you can change it whenever you want, instantly, even in the middle of a sentence.

08

Quick definition, because people use this word a lot of ways. For our purposes, a harness is the tooling around an LLM that gets it to do what we want it to do, better. The model is in the middle. The harness is everything around it.

09

My contention is that there are things specific to thinking that need a different kind of harness. Not because coding is simple — good coding tools brainstorm and explore goals too. It’s that thinking sits upstream. A thinking harness can ask: should we write code at all? Is this problem upstream of that one? The result might be code, handed to a coding harness. Or a story, a decision — or nothing to build. And a few things are specific to thinking: there’s no set destination. Success is that you understand something new, which the AI can’t do for you. The moves — extract, expand, challenge, shape — come in any order, over and over. And there’s nothing to run: you can execute code and watch what happens; you can’t execute an idea, so you have to track what you’re trusting.

10

Here’s what it might look like. First, you pick the kind of thinking you want right now. Find what I mean, clarify, expand, challenge, make it usable. Here I’ve picked Expand — so when I say newsrooms have something to teach us, it makes the idea bigger. It doesn’t rush to a plan, it doesn’t grade me.

11

Within a mode, you set the dials. How much should it affirm versus challenge me? Keep exploring, or move toward a solution? Grounded or wild? A fast exchange or deep work? And how much should it do on its own without asking? Here: exploring, fairly wild, quick, gentle on the criticism for now.

12

Halfway through its answer, I tap Challenge. It stops mid-sentence and changes course — right now, not on the next turn. And nothing else moves: it’s still exploring, still wild, still fast. Asking for more pushback doesn’t mean it gets to start solving. That’s the guarantee: it holds my settings, and it changes instantly when I change them.

13

While I keep thinking, other work runs alongside. One agent asks whether I’m even asking the right question. One goes and finds research and examples. One tries completely different approaches. It doesn’t interrupt me — but it doesn’t disappear, either. It sits here, ready when I want it.

14

This is the hardest problem. When a conversation goes bad, I start fresh — and lose the work. If I carry everything forward, I carry the bad habits and wrong assumptions too. Worse: it generates documents I don’t fully read. I approve one, and a wrong assumption in it becomes the foundation for everything after. So the harness should keep track of what it’s assuming, and where each assumption came from: did I say it, did it propose it, did I accept it, did anyone verify it? And it should show me only the few that matter, at a volume I can actually check. Approved doesn’t mean read. Read doesn’t mean true.

15

Here’s the same thing as a command line, the way a lot of people in this room already work with Claude Code. I start in Expand. Halfway through, I switch to Challenge — and it says so: dials unchanged. I turn up the pushback. Three agents are running alongside: one reframing the question, one doing research, one drafting other approaches. It flags an assumption it made on its own — that the goal is a product. I reject it, and it tells me what depended on it. And the status line always shows where the settings are.

16

Here’s a version I actually want on my desk. The harness is on the screen. Little ESP32 displays show the state at a glance: how hard it’s pushing back, where every dial is, what the agents are doing, and how many assumptions are waiting for me. Real knobs, a little steering wheel and a joystick let me turn the dials by hand without breaking my train of thought. And instead of typing a mode, I pick up a figure — the editor, the fact-checker, the wild one, the outsider — and set it on the NFC pad. That’s who I’m talking to now.

17

The good news: most of this is hard, but buildable today. Holding the mode means the harness restates it every turn and a fast checker catches replies that break it. Switching mid-turn means stop and restart in the new mode, keeping what was written — it feels instant. Independent dials come from separate agents. Creative reach comes from generating lots and selecting for distance from the obvious. Background agents run in parallel. And the memory and assumption problems are solvable if the system records where every claim came from as it’s written.

18

And what isn’t possible yet — what needs changes to the models themselves or the architecture. True steering in the middle of generation: today it’s stop and restart. Guaranteed obedience: models are probabilistic, so reliability has to come from outside checks. Honest self-reports: a model can’t reliably tell you what it actually assumed, and the deepest framing never shows up in the text at all. It can’t forget part of a session in place. Memory is notes it reads back, not learning your culture. And it doesn’t know how sure it is.

19

So here’s the takeaway. Switching mid-turn is mostly an API limit — that will get solved. Verification is the deeper problem. And we already know how to handle that from journalism: you don’t ask the reporter whether the story is true. The fact-checker goes back to the sources. The system should record where every claim came from, instead of trusting the model’s account of itself.

20

Now we switch to workshop mode. First, quickly: who helps you think well, and what are they actually doing? Then let’s pick one real thinking task and build its harness on this board. I filled in one example per column — “is there a story here?” — the rest is yours. What task? What modes does it need? Which dials, set where? What must it never do? What should run alongside you? How does it handle trust? Anything we can’t solve goes in the parking lot.
